title: S Janaki, the Nightingale of South India, Dies at 88 After Recording 48,000 Songs Across Six Decades
excerpt: The legendary playback singer, who lent her voice to films in 17 languages and won four National Awards, passed away in Mysuru on July 11.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • S Janaki, legendary playback singer, died at 88 in Mysuru on July 11.
  • She recorded approximately 48,000 songs in 17 languages over six decades.
  • Janaki won four National Film Awards and declined the Padma Bhushan in 2013.
  • Tributes from PM Modi and President Murmu mark her death as an end of an era.
  • Legendary playback singer S Janaki died at 88 in Mysuru on July 11 after experiencing breathing difficulties related to age
  • Over a career spanning more than six decades, Janaki recorded approximately 48,000 songs in 17 languages including Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Hindi
  • She won the National Film Award for Best Female Playback Singer four times and declined the Padma Bhushan in 2013
  • Prime Minister Modi, President Murmu and leading figures across Indian cinema paid tribute, calling her death the end of an era in Indian music

S Janaki, the playback singer whose extraordinary voice defined generations of South Indian cinema, died on July 11 at a private hospital in Mysuru. She was 88. Her granddaughter Apsara Vydyula confirmed the death in an Instagram post, saying she "left us peacefully, surrounded by the love of her family."

Hospital sources said Janaki developed breathing difficulties on the evening of July 10 and was admitted for treatment. She died the following day from age-related ailments and cardiac arrest.

A Voice That Transcended Languages

Born on April 23, 1938, in Guntur district of Andhra Pradesh, Janaki had no formal training in classical music. Her journey began after she placed second in an All India Radio national music competition in 1956. A year later, at 19, she made her playback debut in the Tamil film Vidhiyin Vilayattu.

What followed was one of the most prolific recording careers in Indian music history. Janaki recorded approximately 48,000 songs across 17 languages — predominantly Kannada, Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam, but also Hindi, Odia, Tulu, Urdu, Punjabi and Bengali. Kannada accounted for the largest share of her recordings.

"To the world, she was an iconic voice whose songs became part of countless memories. To us, she was a loving grandmother whose warmth, humility, kindness and grace will remain with us forever."

— Apsara Vydyula, granddaughter

Her Hindi film contributions included memorable songs like Bol Baby Bol from Meri Jung, Prabhu More Avgun from Sur Sangam, and O Maria from Saagar. She collaborated with some of Indian cinema's greatest composers, including M.S. Viswanathan, Ilaiyaraaja and A.R. Rahman.

Awards, Honours, and a Declined Padma Bhushan

Janaki won the National Film Award for Best Female Playback Singer four times — for Sindhoora Poove (1976), Ettumanoor Ambalathil (1980), Vennello Godari (1984) and Inji Iduppazhaga (1992). She received multiple state awards from Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh.

In 2013, when the Indian government announced it would confer the Padma Bhushan — the country's third-highest civilian honour — Janaki declined to accept it. She never publicly explained her reasons, but the decision added to her reputation as an artist unconcerned with institutional recognition.

Farewell With Full State Honours

Janaki's mortal remains were brought to Maharaja's College Grounds in Mysuru on July 12 for public viewing, where thousands of fans gathered to pay their respects. Her last rites were performed at her ancestral farmhouse in HD Kote taluk, Mysuru, following traditional Telugu Brahmin customs. Her granddaughter Apsara lit the funeral pyre.

The Karnataka government accorded her a state funeral.

A Legacy for the Diaspora

For the millions of South Indians living abroad, Janaki's voice is the soundtrack of home. Her songs have been played at weddings, festivals and family gatherings across the diaspora for decades. From Thaliritta Kinakkal in Malayalam to Thumbi Vaa Thumbikkudathin and countless Tamil and Kannada film classics, her recordings bridged the distance between NRIs and the culture they carried with them.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi said her voice "beautifully conveyed every emotion to the people." President Droupadi Murmu called her "an invaluable treasure of the Indian music world." Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge said her "golden voice transcended several languages and generations."

What Her Passing Means

Tributes to a Musical Icon
›PM Modi: Her voice conveyed every emotion.
›President Murmu: An invaluable treasure of Indian music.
›Kharge: Her voice transcended languages and generations.

With Janaki's death, coming just three months after Asha Bhosle's passing in April, India has lost two of its most defining playback voices within the same year. Janaki's career was remarkable not just for its scale — 48,000 songs is a number difficult to fully comprehend — but for the consistent emotional depth she brought to each recording, whether it was a devotional bhajan, a romantic melody or a folk song.

She leaves behind a body of work that will continue to define South Indian cinema for generations to come.
